name: Sam Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing business and management, with an entrepreneurship stream. My week is two lectures, a team project where we're pitching a fake startup, and a lot of time in the library cafe working on my own shop. I sell custom sticker packs online, and I use AI for designs, product descriptions and answering customers. Evenings I work three shifts at an electronics store called Volt.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And how does money work for you right now, between family, the part-time job and the course?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My parents run a pizzeria in Turin, and they pay my rent in a shared flat, but not much beyond that. I live on the store wage and what the sticker shop brings in, usually 150 a week all together. It's not a fortune, but I don't feel poor, and I keep two months' worth of costs in a savings account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here is the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fine, it's still handy. It already saves me about ten hours a week on my shop, so even a plateau helps. I'd tell the guys at Volt, my store, that not every new thing needs to be a revolution.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm relaxed, because I've already got what I need from the tools I use. If they stay as they are, I keep my shop, my degree and my shifts. The only thing is that if everything stays the same, I have to find my edge another way, because I won't win just by being early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running the shop, add a second product line like phone cases, and use the weekends to test a small ad budget, maybe 30 a month. I'd stay on the degree and apply for a startup summer programme. I'd also save 40 a week, because I like having a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the cosy version, where I can keep tinkering and nothing comes crashing down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your sticker shop leans on AI. What happens if the tools stop improving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd be one of many people using the same tools, so I'd have to be better at the human parts: picking designs people like, talking to customers, finding a niche. Honestly that's fine, it's what business is really about anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the time you'd otherwise spend worrying?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend it testing ideas. Last month I tried a design for a local football club, and it sold out in two days. That sort of experiment is worth more than any amount of worrying.

say: I'd tell my colleagues at Volt that not every new thing needs to be a **revolution**.
I'd say even a plateau helps, since AI already saves me ten hours a **week**.
think: If tools stay as they are, I keep my shop, my degree and my **shifts**.
I'd have to find my **edge** another way, because being early won't win.
do: Add a second product line like phone cases and test a **30 a month** ad budget.
Apply for a startup **summer programme** and save 40 a week.
feel: **Calm**, the cosy version where I can keep tinkering.

fieldNote: He is **calm** because he already earns and tests ideas, not because the world is safe.
He thinks a plateau would force him to compete on human skills.
He saves 40 a week despite relaxed talk, which shows a steady cushion habit.

steps.text: Launch a phone case line in the sticker shop this term
Save 40 a week into a separate account
Spend 30 a month testing small ads for the shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next picture, called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big opportunity if you move early, and a big problem if you wait. I'd say that to my course mates and online, and offer to show people how I use the tools in my shop. I'd also say the government should fund training so it isn't only people like me who benefit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think a lot of ordinary business jobs shrink, like admin, bookkeeping and customer service. I'm in a course that trains people for exactly that. But I'm also running a small business, so I think I'm on the right side of it, as long as I keep learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build my sticker shop into something real, use AI to handle customer chats and ads, and take on one or two small clients to design for. I'd take a short online course on automation. I'd save 60 a week and keep one week of shifts at Volt, in case the shop slows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My own job and income look okay, but I can see plenty of people around me who might be hit, and that's on my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would your own course feel the squeeze in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents' pizzeria. They already use an ordering app and a delivery platform, and each one takes a cut. If AI makes ordering even more of a platform business, the margin could shrink. I'd talk them into building their own simple ordering page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your family would notice the change first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My course, honestly. A lot of what we study is exactly what these tools do: finance basics, reports, marketing copy. My lecturers know, and they're all slightly uneasy. We joke about it in class, which is a bit nervous.

I'd say government should fund **training** so it's not only people like me who benefit.

Running a small **business** puts me on the right side, if I keep learning.
do: Build the sticker shop into something **real** and take one or two design clients.
Take an online course on **automation** and keep a week of Volt shifts as backup.
feel: **Uneasy**: my income looks okay but people around me may be hit.
S1.quote: I'd build my sticker shop into something real, use AI to handle customer chats and ads, and take on one or two small clients to design for.
fieldNote: He sees his course as training for exactly the **tasks** AI takes, and says so.
He worries about the pizzeria's margins when delivery platforms take a cut.
His adaptive streak shows in plans that are specific and low-cost.

steps.text: Take two small design clients for the sticker shop
Finish an online course on workflow automation
Set up AI chat replies and ad tests for the shop
Help my parents build their own pizzeria ordering page

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the picture called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this changes everything, and we need to be smart and quick. I'd tell my friends to try the tools, and I'd tell my lecturers to rewrite the course now, not in three years. And I'd say to the government: set up a safety net before, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel more nervous than I expect. I can tinker, but I'm 18, with a degree that will take three more years, and a shop that depends on tools that would suddenly be everywhere. If anyone can make stickers with AI, my edge goes to nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build as fast as I can: more products, more channels, and a list of customers who really like my designs. I'd try to get a place on a startup programme. I'd save as much as possible, and I'd check what my parents' pizzeria would do if people start ordering from robot kitchens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's an adrenaline kind of worry, not a freeze kind. I'd be busy, but I'd also feel scared late at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's different about two years for someone who loves trying new tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them that restaurants are hands-on, so they're safer for a while, but the ordering, scheduling and supplier side will change fast. I'd push them to adopt tools early so they don't lose money, and to keep savings for the lean months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents about the pizzeria?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I can't be careful. I'd be trying everything at once, hoping a few ideas stick. That's more tiring than exciting, I think, and I might make mistakes with money I can't afford to lose.

say: I'd tell my lecturers to rewrite the course now, not in **three years**.
I'd ask the government to set up a **safety net** before, not after.
think: If anyone can make stickers with AI, my **edge** goes to nothing.

do: Launch **more products** and build a list of customers who like my designs.
Apply to a **startup programme** and save as much as possible.
feel: **Anxious**, with adrenaline in the day and fear late at night.
S2.quote: With two years I can't be careful. I'd be trying everything at once, hoping a few ideas stick.
fieldNote: His tinkering streak becomes **frantic** when time is short, and he knows it.
He worries he'd lose money he can't afford to lose.
He thinks the pizzeria is safer short-term but its back-office work would change first.

steps.text: Launch three new sticker lines in the next two months
Save 80 a week and cut eating out to once a month
Set up AI order handling for the sticker shop
Ask a startup programme mentor to review my plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the picture called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a race, but it's one you can plan for. I'd tell friends to build real skills and a bit of money, not just chase the hype. I'd probably post about how I'm using the tools, to be open about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel good. In five years I'd have the degree and maybe a small company. It's hard, but I'd be one of the people who built something during the change instead of being surprised by it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree and grow the shop into a small brand with a few products. I'd use AI for almost everything and take a part-time job in a startup to learn how others do it. I'd invest around 50 a month in an index fund, because I want something growing that I don't have to run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but upbeat. It's a bit like starting a hard hike: you know it'll hurt, but you've got time to train.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with five years that you couldn't do with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years, I'd actually use the whole degree. I'd pick the modules on finance, law and strategy, because owning a company needs those and the tools don't replace judgement. The degree is the base, the shop is the lab.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your degree still matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The difference is I can sleep. Two years is sprint, five is a season. I can pick the best experiments instead of running every one.

fieldNote: Five years turns his **frenzy** into a season of picked experiments.

steps.text: Grow the sticker shop into a small branded range
Invest 50 a month in an index fund
Pick finance, law and strategy modules for second year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last picture, called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's all very exciting and a bit slow. I'd say let's use the ten years to get things right: teach people the tools, build the safety nets, and let people try things. I'd tell my friends to start small and learn by doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm fairly calm. A decade is long enough to build and sell a business, or to work for a couple of firms and learn. The thing I'd keep in mind is that tools get stronger every year, so I can't stay still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd graduate, run my own business or work in a startup, and move into whatever grows. I'd probably do a master's if it helps. I'd keep investing about 60 a month. I'd also set up a small online ordering system for my parents' pizzeria so they're ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit impatient. I'd want to get going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With a decade, would you still run a sticker shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not stickers, the shop is a start. I'd build something bigger by then, maybe a service for small restaurants like my parents', using AI to handle ordering and supplies. That feels like a natural idea, and I'd test it in the pizzeria first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you feel about your parents' pizzeria in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel okay, as long as they've got savings and aren't relying on the old way. Hands-on work will last longer, and a good pizza is a good pizza, but the business around it will change, and I'd want to be the one helping my parents with it.

say: I'd say let's use ten years to teach people the tools and build **safety nets**.
I'd tell friends to **start small** and learn by doing.
think: A decade is long enough to **build** and sell a business or learn at a few firms.
Tools get stronger every year, so I **can't** stand still.

Set up a simple online **ordering** system for my parents' pizzeria.

S4.quote: A good pizza is a good pizza, but the business around it will change, and I'd want to be the one helping my parents with it.
fieldNote: With a decade he imagines a **service for small restaurants**, built from his parents' pizzeria.

steps.text: Test an AI ordering service for small restaurants at the pizzeria
Invest 60 a month in a diversified fund

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it's so fast that it breaks the whole idea of a starting plan. I'm usually the one who says, let's try it, and even I don't know what I'd try. What would help is a bit of structure: where to learn, who to ask, and a way to keep earning while I work it out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether I'd actually want it to happen. I get excited about the tools, but I also hate the idea of my parents' pizzeria being worth less because everyone orders from a robot kitchen. I'd say I'm optimistic and nervous at once, and I don't think those cancel each other out.

headlineQuote: I'm optimistic and nervous at once, and I don't think those cancel each other out.
portrait: Sam is 18 and studies **business and management**, runs a small online sticker shop and works evenings at an electronics store.
His parents run a **pizzeria** and cover part of his rent; he uses AI tools every day.
He is a centrist and a tinkerer who blames nobody and prefers to **test things** and see what works.
His mood stays calm in slow worlds and turns anxious when time is short, because he has **no plan** for two years.
He moves first on tools and money, then asks his family and teachers how to fit things together.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028** most, since it is so fast it breaks the idea of making a plan.
whatWouldHelp: He wants some **structure**: where to learn, who to ask, and a way to keep earning while he works it out.
